seq = ['RIGHT','RIGHT','UP','SPACE','DOWN','LEFT','LEFT']

    # report carrying state
    nodes = current_frame.segmentation['nodes']
    N=[n for n in nodes if n['color']=='N'][0]
    W=[n for n in nodes if n['color']=='W']

        rs=[p[0] for p in n['boundary']];cs=[p[1] for p in n['boundary']]

    print(a,'N',bb(N),'W',[(n['pixels'],bb(n)) for n in W])
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

Key findings from full transition trace:
- Player = 4×4 box (12 green + 4 white "head"). Head sits on the side of last successful move (top after UP, bottom after DOWN, right after RIGHT); while carrying a frame the head is pinned on top.
- SPACE below a frame (frame directly above head) = pick up (frame→white, attaches above head). SPACE while carrying = drop in place (frame→gray, reverts to normal frame, merges with adjacent frames). That's why B+C merged into a 4×8 double frame at cols 16-23.
- Carried frame rides 4 rows above green; it can overlap the bar's row without docking (T6 just occluded the bar, which fully restored when the frame moved away). So docking is NOT achieved by carrying over a slot.
- Open question: does dropping (SPACE) a frame while aligned on a bar slot dock it?
Plan: use clean frame A (24-27,44-47) as a docking probe — carry it to the bar's right slot (36-39) and drop it, observe whether the bar changes permanently.
